stages.title: Advanced linguistics and grammar
stages.hook: Is "Colourless green ideas sleep furiously" grammatical? It is nonsense in meaning, yet it feels like English.
explain: Linguistics studies language scientifically. Its main levels are phonetics and phonology (sounds), morphology (word structure), syntax (sentence structure), semantics (meaning) and pragmatics (meaning in context). Noam Chomsky's example sentence shows that grammaticality and meaning are separate.

A morpheme is the smallest unit of meaning: "unhappiness" has three (un-, happy, -ness). Syntax describes how words group into phrases, shown in tree diagrams. Pragmatics explains why "Can you pass the salt?" is a request and not a question about ability. Descriptive grammar records how people speak; prescriptive grammar states how they should.
stages.mnemonic: Sounds, words, sentences, meaning, use: the five layers.
items: the study of meaning in context
the study of meaning of words
a rule-based description of real usage
a rule saying how people should speak
the smallest sound unit that changes meaning
sentences: Syntax studies how words form phrases.

gq.q: "Can you open the window?" is usually understood as...
gq.why: Pragmatics: the speaker's intention differs from the literal meaning.

panel.q: /p/ and /b/ are different phonemes in English because...
o: swapping them changes the word, as in pat and bat
they are both vowels and vowels always change meaning
panel.why: A minimal pair shows that a sound distinction signals meaning.

panel.q: What is the difference between descriptive and prescriptive grammar?
panel.model: Descriptive grammar records how people actually use language; prescriptive grammar lays down how they should use it.
panel.why: Two attitudes to grammar.

panel.q: Chomsky's sentence about colourless green ideas shows that...
o: a sentence can be grammatical without making sense
meaning always decides whether a sentence is grammatical
panel.why: It separates syntax from semantics.

teach.model: Linguists study language in layers: sounds, word parts, sentence structure, meaning, and use in context. A morpheme is the smallest meaningful unit. Grammar can describe real use or prescribe a standard.

points.ask: Is grammar a description or a rule?

stages.title: Historical development of the language
stages.hook: Why is English spelt "knight" but pronounced "nite"? The answer lies in history.
explain: English is a West Germanic language. Old English (about 450-1100) was brought by Anglo-Saxon settlers. After the Norman Conquest of 1066 French influenced Middle English (about 1100-1500), producing many pairs like cow/beef and pig/pork. Chaucer wrote in Middle English.

Early Modern English, the time of Shakespeare and the King James Bible (1611), was shaped by the printing press and the Great Vowel Shift (roughly 1400-1700), when long vowels changed. Spelling was fixed by printing before the shift finished, which is why spelling and sound often do not match. Johnson's dictionary (1755) strengthened standardisation. Today English keeps absorbing words, from Arabic ("algebra"), Hindi ("jungle") and many other languages.
stages.mnemonic: Old, Middle, Modern: three stages, two big shocks: 1066 and the vowel shift.
items: a change in long vowels c. 1400-1700
a word taken from another language
the study of where words come from

gq.q: Which event strongly influenced Middle English vocabulary?
gq.why: French became the language of the ruling class, adding many words.

o: Germanic farmers' word and French-derived food word
a spelling error that was never corrected in the dictionary
gq.why: A traditional explanation is that English-speaking farmers kept the animals while Norman French speakers ate the meat, so the French-derived word names the food.

panel.q: Why is English spelling irregular?
o: Spelling was largely standardised before sounds finished changing
Spelling was invented only in the twentieth century by a few teachers
panel.why: Printing fixed spellings during the Great Vowel Shift and many loanwords kept their original spellings.

panel.q: Why does English have so many loanwords?
panel.model: Through conquest, trade, empire and migration, English came into contact with many languages and borrowed words from them.
panel.why: Language contact.

panel.q: Which word is a Hindi loanword in English?
panel.why: Jungle comes from Hindi jangal; algebra is from Arabic, guitar from Spanish/Greek, tsunami from Japanese.

teach.model: English began as Old English in the 5th century. French changed it after 1066, creating Middle English. Printing and the Great Vowel Shift explain why spelling and sound differ. English keeps borrowing words.

stages.title: Literature and cultural discourse
stages.hook: Why is "To be, or not to be" still quoted? What does a culture do with its stories?
explain: Literature joins a cultural conversation. Canonical works such as Shakespeare, Austen, Dickens, Achebe, Walcott, Morrison and Rushdie are read, taught and challenged. Postcolonial writers such as Chinua Achebe write English in ways that carry African voices and idioms. The idea of the canon is debated: who decides which books are important?

Critical approaches include formalist (focus on form), historical, feminist, postcolonial and reader-response readings. Intertextuality means that texts echo other texts. Discourse analysis examines how language shapes social meaning, for example in politics or advertising. Present competing readings and justify yours with evidence.
stages.mnemonic: Every text talks to other texts.
items: the works widely taught as important
reading shaped by the reader's response

gq.q: How many lines does a sonnet traditionally have?

o: The way texts refer to or echo other texts
A kind of spelling variation found in very old books
gq.why: A modern poem alluding to Shakespeare is intertextual.

panel.q: Why is the literary canon debated?
o: Selection reflects choices that may exclude voices
Because books are expensive and few people can buy them
Because all books are equal in length
panel.why: Which works are included reflects power and taste, so critics ask whose voices are missing.

panel.q: How can different critics read the same novel in different ways?
panel.model: Each critic uses a different lens, such as feminist or postcolonial, and supports a reading with textual evidence.
panel.why: Plural interpretations.

panel.q: Chinua Achebe's "Things Fall Apart" is an important novel from...
panel.why: Achebe was a Nigerian novelist and the book was published in 1958.

teach.model: Literature is part of a long conversation between texts and readers. Critics use different lenses to read a work. Ask which voices are included in the canon and which are not.

points.ask: How do I back my reading?

stages.title: Advanced academic writing
stages.hook: What is the difference between "This proves X" and "This is consistent with X"? Academic writers care a lot.
explain: Advanced academic writing builds an argument supported by sources. A strong thesis is arguable and specific. Use a research question, a literature review (what is known), a method, results and discussion. Position your work: "Whereas Smith (2018) argues..., this essay contends that..."

Control stance with hedges and boosters ("may", "clearly"), and cohesive devices such as nominal groups ("this finding"). Use citation styles consistently, such as APA or Harvard. Avoid unsupported generalisations and rhetorical questions. Edit for concision, parallelism and clear referencing.
stages.mnemonic: Say what is known, say what is missing, say what you add.
items: a word that makes a claim less certain
the way a source is credited
a statement that goes beyond evidence
sentences: This essay contends that policy matters.
The findings may indicate a trend.

gq.q: Which claim is most appropriately cautious?
o: The results appear to indicate a link.
There is clearly always a link between them.
gq.why: Hedging matches the strength of the claim to the evidence.

gq.q: What does a literature review do?
o: Shows what is already known and identifies a gap
Lists the writer's personal opinions about the topic and nothing else
gq.why: It situates the research in earlier work.

panel.q: Which is an arguable thesis?
o: Remote working improves productivity in some sectors but not others.
Remote working began in recent years and is now very common in many countries.
panel.why: An arguable thesis takes a debatable position that evidence can support.

panel.q: Why is it important to cite sources consistently in a recognised style?
panel.model: It credits earlier work, avoids plagiarism, and lets readers verify and find the sources.
panel.why: Scholarly integrity.

panel.q: Which phrasing positions your argument against another scholar?
o: While Smith argues X, this essay contends Y.
Smith wrote an interesting article about X last year.
panel.why: It acknowledges the earlier view and states a distinct claim.

teach.model: A good academic text asks a question, reviews earlier research and makes a clear, arguable claim. It is supported by evidence and cited sources. Use cautious language so that your claims fit your evidence.

stages.title: Professional translation
stages.hook: A contract says "shall". A friend's text says "shall we?". Could a translator confuse them?
explain: Professional translation covers legal, medical, technical and literary texts. Each needs terminology, a consistent style and knowledge of the subject. Translators use glossaries, translation memory tools, style guides and quality checks such as revision by a second translator. Machine translation is useful as a first draft but needs post-editing by a human.

Legal English uses "shall" for obligations: "The tenant shall pay rent monthly." Plain-English reform advises "must". Accuracy, confidentiality and meeting deadlines are core to the profession. Decide on terminology early and apply it consistently. Cultural adaptation (localisation) covers dates, units, humour and names.
stages.mnemonic: Know the field, keep a glossary, check twice.
items: a second translator checks the work
the full set of rules for a project style
an official translation with a signed statement
sentences: The tenant shall pay rent monthly.

gq.q: Which tool helps keep terminology consistent?
gq.why: Agreed term lists ensure the same concept is rendered the same way.
Shall in a contract imposes a duty.

panel.q: Why is machine translation output usually post-edited for important documents?
o: It may contain errors in nuance, terms or context
It is never accurate, so it must always be rewritten
panel.why: Errors in register, terminology and ambiguity can be costly.

panel.q: Why is confidentiality an important ethical duty for translators?
panel.model: Documents often contain sensitive legal, medical or business information, and clients must be able to trust that it will not be shared.
panel.why: Professional ethics.

panel.q: A US product label shows "12 fl oz" and the date "12/31/24" for a UK market. This needs...
o: localisation of units and date format
translation of the nouns on the label only
panel.why: Units and date formats should follow local conventions: about 355 ml and 31/12/24.

teach.model: Professional translators work in a field such as law or medicine. They use glossaries to keep terms consistent. They check their work and keep documents private. Machine translation needs human checking.

points.ask: How do you keep terms the same?

stages.title: Interpretation of complex communication
stages.hook: "We should perhaps consider alternatives." Is that a suggestion, a warning or a refusal? How does a skilled interpreter decide?
explain: Complex communication carries meaning beyond words: implicature, politeness, irony, cultural references and silence. In diplomacy, "We will study the proposal carefully" can signal polite refusal. Paul Grice proposed maxims of quantity, quality, relation and manner; speakers flout them to imply meaning.

Interpreters analyse the speaker's intent, register and audience. They may need to explain cultural references briefly, and to manage turn-taking and emotion. In critical settings (courts, healthcare) accuracy matters more than smoothing, and interpreters should say when they need clarification. Face-saving and honorifics differ across cultures.
stages.mnemonic: Listen for what is said, what is meant and what is left unsaid.
items: a rule of cooperative conversation, like be relevant
to break a conversational rule on purpose
sentences: We will study the proposal carefully.
She answered indirectly to save face.

gq.q: If A asks "Are you coming to the party?" and B says "I have an exam tomorrow", B probably means...
gq.why: The relevance of the exam implies a refusal: this is an implicature.

gq.q: Who proposed the conversational maxims of quantity, quality, relation and manner?
gq.why: Grice described how speakers cooperate in conversation.

panel.q: Why might a literal interpretation of "We will study this carefully" mislead a negotiator?
o: It can be a polite way of declining
It always means yes, so the negotiator can relax
panel.why: Indirectness is a face-saving strategy in many cultures.

panel.q: When should an interpreter ask for clarification rather than guess?
panel.model: When a statement is unclear or ambiguous and an error could matter, especially in legal or medical settings.
panel.why: Accuracy over fluency in high-stakes contexts.

panel.q: Which is a risk of rendering a polite refusal as a plain "No"?
o: It may damage the relationship by changing tone
It is always more accurate and saves time in every case
panel.why: Interpreters convey meaning and force, not only words.

teach.model: Speakers often mean more than they say. A polite phrase can be a refusal. An interpreter listens for intent, tone and culture. When in doubt about an important point, ask the speaker to clarify.

points.ask: What else should I listen for?
What do I do if unsure?

stages.title: Language variation and dialectology
stages.hook: Is the way your grandparents speak "wrong English"? How do linguists study variety?
explain: Dialectology maps variation in vocabulary, grammar and pronunciation across places (dialects) and groups (sociolects). A dialect is a variety of a language, not a lesser form. An accent concerns only pronunciation. Standard varieties arise from social and political history, not linguistic superiority.

Examples: rhoticity (pronouncing /r/ after vowels, as in General American and Scottish English, but not in most of England), the Northern Cities Vowel Shift in the US, Indian English retroflex consonants, Singlish, and African American English, a rule-governed variety. Code-switching means moving between varieties or languages. Attitudes towards accents can cause bias, which linguists call linguistic discrimination.
stages.mnemonic: A dialect is a language with a different history, not a worse one.
items: a regional variety of a language
a variety linked to a social group
a variety accepted for formal use
sentences: A dialect is not a lesser language.

gq.q: What is the difference between a dialect and an accent?
o: A dialect includes vocabulary and grammar; an accent is pronunciation
An accent includes vocabulary and grammar; a dialect is only pronunciation
gq.why: Accent concerns sound, dialect covers more.

gq.q: Which feature describes pronouncing /r/ at the end of "car"?
gq.why: Rhotic accents pronounce the r after vowels.

panel.q: Why do linguists reject the idea that a standard variety is linguistically superior?
o: Standards are social choices; all varieties have complex rules
Standards are much older than all other dialects, so they are better
panel.why: The prestige of a variety comes from social power, not linguistic features.

panel.q: Why might someone code-switch between varieties?
panel.model: People adapt to the audience or setting and express identity or solidarity.
panel.why: Sociolinguistic motivation.

panel.q: African American English is best described as...
o: a rule-governed variety with its own systematic features
a collection of errors made by people who did not learn English well
panel.why: Linguists study it as a systematic variety.

teach.model: A dialect is a variety of a language with its own words and grammar. An accent is only about how words sound. All dialects follow rules, and none is wrong in itself. People may change their speech for different groups.

stages.title: Specialised scientific or technical language
stages.hook: Why do scientists write "the sample was heated" and not "I heated the sample"?
explain: Scientific and technical English uses precise terminology, many noun phrases ("temperature-dependent reaction rate"), passive voice in methods, and hedging in discussion. Abbreviations and units follow standards: SI units, with a space between number and unit. Terms are often built from Greek and Latin roots (thermo-, hydro-, -ology).

Scientific papers follow IMRaD: Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion. Clear definitions matter: "significant" in statistics means unlikely to be due to chance, not merely important. Technical writing, such as manuals, uses short imperative steps and consistent terms. Visuals need captions that explain what to notice.
stages.mnemonic: IMRaD: Introduce, Method, Results, and Discussion.
items: the standard structure of a scientific paper
the way an experiment was done
a number with unit, e.g. 5 kg
a term used in one field
sentences: The sample was heated to 80 degrees Celsius.

gq.q: Which section of a paper describes how an experiment was done?
gq.why: Methods lets others repeat the study.

gq.q: Why is the passive often used in methods sections?
o: The action matters more than the person
Passives are always shorter than active sentences
gq.why: Focus is on the procedure, not who did it.

panel.q: In a statistics report "a significant difference" means...
o: unlikely to have arisen by chance
large and important enough to matter in practice
panel.why: Statistical significance is a technical term and is not the same as practical importance.

panel.q: Why is consistent terminology essential in technical manuals?
panel.model: Using the same term for the same thing avoids confusion and errors, which matters especially for safety instructions.
panel.why: Precision and safety.

panel.q: Which is the clearest manual instruction?
o: Turn off the power before opening the cover.
The power should maybe be off.
Power off sometimes helps if the cover is hard to open
panel.why: Imperatives in a logical order are the standard for instructions.

teach.model: Scientific writing is precise and formal. A paper follows a standard order: introduction, methods, results, discussion. Technical manuals use short commands and the same word for the same thing every time.

stages.title: Integrated proficiency project
stages.hook: Can you bring together everything you know - sounds, grammar, register, culture - in one real project?
explain: The integrated project combines skills: research, reading sources, discussing, writing and presenting. A sample task: investigate how a word or expression varies across English varieties, then report findings in a short article and a five-minute talk. Organise with a research question, collect examples, compare them, and draw careful conclusions.

Assess your own proficiency with a framework such as the CEFR (Common European Framework of Reference for Languages), which describes levels A1 to C2. At C1 and C2 users handle complex texts, express ideas fluently and adjust register. Reflect: what did you do well, which errors persist, and what will you practise next?
items: to look at similarities and differences
to think about your own learning
to give a short spoken report
sentences: I collected examples from three varieties.
I will practise my weaker areas.

gq.q: How many main levels does the CEFR have?
o: Six (A1, A2, B1, B2, C1, C2)
gq.why: The CEFR has six levels from A1 to C2.

gq.q: What should come first in a research project?
o: The final conclusion written before collecting any data
gq.why: The question guides data collection and analysis.

panel.q: A learner finds only two examples of a word and states a rule for all of English. What is the error?
o: Using the passive voice too often in a report
panel.why: Conclusions must match the amount and range of evidence.

panel.q: Why is reflection useful in language learning?
panel.model: It shows your progress, strengths and persistent errors, so that you can set goals and plan practice.
panel.why: Metacognition supports learning.

panel.q: Which output best combines reading, writing and speaking in one project?
o: A researched article plus a short presentation
A long vocabulary list with translations in the margin
panel.why: An integrated task uses several skills for a real purpose.

teach.model: A project uses reading, writing, speaking and listening together. Start with a question, collect examples, compare them and report results carefully. Then reflect on what you can do and what to practise next.
